_README: Approach variants — Stuart Range / Enchantments, 2026-08-19. 30 routes, 32 variants, every one carrying a baseFinding.
`area` on every entry was READ FROM THE LIVE ROW (routes.area_id), not typed from the route name. Nine of these
ids carry no peak name at all — wa_south_face_12 is Argonaut, wa_northeast_buttress_4 is Colchuck Peak,
wa_e_se_face is Witches Tower, wa_the_tipping_point is Colchuck Balanced Rock, wa_beckey_davis /
wa_stanley_burgner / wa_boving_christensen / wa_energizer_bunny are Prusik, wa_sherpa_glacier is filed under
MOUNT STUART (correctly — the Sherpa Glacier is on Stuart, not on Sherpa Peak) — and a name-shaped id is not
evidence of which peak you are on.
Scope was the 13 named peaks plus the two sub-feature areas the catalog files beneath them
(wa_sherpa_balanced_rock, wa_colchuck_balanced_rock). 45 routes in those areas had an EMPTY approach_variants;
30 are written here and 15 were deliberately skipped — see _SKIPPED.
Contamination rejected during research, recorded so it is not re-introduced:
- 'Northeast Buttress' and 'Northeast Couloir' both exist on Colchuck Peak AND on other Mountain Project
areas in the Northwest Region and British Columbia. Only the Central-East Cascades / Colchuck Peak pages
were used.
- 'North Ridge' on Sherpa Peak vs the North Ridge of Mount Stuart vs a North Ridge on Sherpa Balanced Rock —
three different lines in one basin. Each was matched by FA party and pitch count, not by name.
- Mount Stuart carries a DB row named 'North Face' whose own beta says no such named route exists on the
mountain. No variant was written for it; see _SKIPPED and _DEFECTS.
- Ingalls Creek and Ingalls Peak are two different places sharing a name in the same approach paragraph;
the Gorillas wall is reached past Ingalls LAKE, the Cascadian and South Headwall from Ingalls CREEK.
No time, distance or gain figure is averaged. Where two sources disagreed, the field is omitted.

approach_variants.name: Mountaineer Creek to the hanging valley, then straight to the toe of the ridge
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Early season the moat at the toe is filled and the walk-in is snow; late season the moat opens and the last few metres onto rock can be the awkward part of the day
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road (about 3,400 ft), follow the trail past the Colchuck Lake fork and keep going. Roughly a mile beyond that fork the maintained trail turns uphill and switchbacks away to the right for Stuart Lake. Leave it there and stay flat in the valley with Mountaineer Creek.

Cross the creek on logs — there is no canonical log and the crossing moves with the snowpack — then follow the south fork upstream. After a couple of miles the valley steepens; turn up a steep talus and boulder slope into the hanging valley beneath Sherpa Peak, where the bivy sites are. That flat ground under the glaciers is the arrival cue for camp.

From the hanging valley the last leg is a faint climbers' path through trees and talus to the moraine, then up the edge of the moraine to rock.

The Direct start is the same climb as the Complete North Ridge with a lower-ridge variation on its first pitches; if you are looking at a row on this app for 'North Ridge (Complete)' as well, treat the approach as identical.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
KEEP THE ICE CLIFF GLACIER ON YOUR LEFT AND WALK UNTIL THE ROCK STOPS YOU. That single sentence is the whole test, and it works in cloud because it is about which side the ice is on rather than about seeing the summit. Climbing out of the hanging valley towards the mountain, the Ice Cliff Glacier must stay on your left the whole way. If it swings round to your right you have walked past the toe and out onto the Stuart Glacier side.

The toe itself is the lowest rock of the ridge, at roughly 6,600 ft, where the moraine runs into the buttress. You are at the correct place when there is nothing lower to climb — the ridge above you rises unbroken and the ground on either side falls away into a glacier.

SECOND TEST, and it is what tells the Direct start from a wander onto the flank: the first belay is off a BIG LEDGE about 150 ft above the base of the toe, with a small tree on it. If you have not passed a big ledge with a tree inside the first rope length, you are not on the line. The three opening pitches are the hardest on the whole route — an awkward squeeze slot and then a long, sustained lieback crack on the left. If your first pitches feel easy, you have started too high and joined the ordinary ridge.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: the ridge you are standing under gains a deep notch with flat bivy ground in it. That notch is where the Upper North Ridge starts, and reaching it on foot means you have skipped the 1,200 ft this route exists for.
hazards: Log crossings of Mountaineer Creek that shift year to year and are worse under early-season snow
Rockfall and icefall off the Ice Cliff Glacier while traversing the moraine beneath it
An open moat between snow and rock at the toe late in the season
Loose rock and crumbly black lichen on the lower pitches
A committing 20-pitch route with the Great Gendarme high on it and no easy retreat once above the lower ridge

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Lake and Goat Pass, traversing east below the Stuart Glacier to the toe
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the Ingalls Way trail is clear and the Stuart Glacier traverse is walkable
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, follow the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass and past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then pick up the climbers' path onto the talus shoulder below Stuart's West Ridge and contour northwest to Goat Pass, about 7,600 ft — the col between Point 7893 and the West Ridge.

This is now the common way parties reach the ridge, and its advantage is that it puts you on the SOUTH side of the range where the descent also finishes, rather than committing you to a north-side camp you then have to walk back around to.

From Goat Pass, do not drop onto the glacier and go up. Traverse EAST below the Stuart Glacier, staying above the large moraine mound, and aim for the toe.

Bivy sites exist at Goat Pass and at Stuart Pass. Published trailhead-to-base times for this variant vary widely enough that no figure is given here.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
STAY ABOVE THE MORAINE MOUND AND KEEP TRAVERSING. Coming from Goat Pass the mistake is vertical, not horizontal: the ground invites you to drop down onto the glacier or to climb up onto the ridge crest early, and both put you on the route above its start.

The line is a rising traverse east, above the large moraine mound below the Stuart Glacier, all the way to the toe. If you find yourself walking DOWN onto flat glacier ice you have dropped too low. If you find yourself scrambling onto ridge crest before you have gone round the end of the rock, you are on the west flank and above the toe.

ARRIVAL: the toe is the point where the buttress runs out into the moraine and there is nothing below it to climb, at roughly 6,600 ft. Confirm it the same way the north-side party does — from the toe, the Ice Cliff Glacier is on the far (east) side of the ridge and the Stuart Glacier is behind you to the west. If both glaciers are on the same side of you, you are not at the toe.

And the same first-pitch check applies: the opening belay is a big ledge with a small tree roughly 150 ft up, and the first three pitches are the hardest of the route. Easy first pitches mean you started too high.
hazards: Crevasses and a soft afternoon snow surface on the Stuart Glacier traverse
Loose moraine and talus on the traverse below the glacier
Route-finding error at Goat Pass in cloud, where dropping onto the glacier feels natural and is wrong
A long committing route with the Great Gendarme high on it
No water between the last melt stream and the summit

approach_variants.name: Goat Pass and the Stuart Glacier to the fourth-class gully and the notch
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; earlier the gully to the notch holds snow and the glacier crossing is simpler, later it is bare and looser
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass, past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then the climbers' path onto the talus shoulder under Stuart's West Ridge and northwest to Goat Pass at about 7,600 ft.

From Goat Pass, traverse ONTO and ACROSS the Stuart Glacier rather than along beneath it, aiming for a fourth-class gully that runs up to the obvious notch in the North Ridge. This is the difference between this route and the complete ridge in one sentence: the complete-ridge party traverses east BELOW the glacier to the toe, this party crosses the glacier and goes UP.

The notch is a bivy: there are two good sites in it, which is why parties who intend to climb the upper ridge in a day from a high camp use it.

Published descriptions of this route are frank that the last of the navigation is yours — one of them says outright to take a topographic map and work it out. Treat that as a real warning rather than as rhetoric.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE NOTCH IS A PLACE YOU CAN SIT DOWN, AND THAT IS THE TEST. There are two good bivy sites in it. If you have arrived somewhere on the crest with no flat ground, you are not at the notch — you have gained the ridge somewhere else along its length.

The approach to it is a fourth-class GULLY off the Stuart Glacier, not a scramble up the ridge flank. If the ground you are climbing is open face rather than a defined gully, you are not in the right line.

ORIENTATION AT THE NOTCH, which settles it: standing in the notch, the whole lower ridge falls away below you to the north and the Ice Cliff Glacier is on the far side of it. Everything above you is the upper ridge, and the Great Gendarme is roughly eight or nine pitches up from here. If the big tower is already below you, you have joined the crest above the notch and above two of the route's three named features.

WHAT YOU HAVE DELIBERATELY GIVEN UP: about 1,200 ft of climbing, including the sustained lieback crack that is the hardest pitch on the complete ridge. So the notch is not a shortcut to be found by accident — a party that meant to climb the complete ridge and ends up here has walked past its own route. Confirm which climb you are on before you start up.
hazards: Crevasses on the Stuart Glacier crossing
Loose rock in the fourth-class gully, with parties above you in it
Knife-edge exposure on the ridge above the notch
The Great Gendarme's offwidth high on the route, with retreat from there awkward
Cold wind on an exposed crest; parties routinely carry bivy kit

approach_variants.name: Reached only by climbing the North Ridge — the base is a point on the route, not a place you walk to
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, as for whichever North Ridge line you are on
approach_variants.notes:
There is no independent approach to this feature. The Great Gendarme is a tower high on Mount Stuart's North Ridge and you arrive at its base having already climbed either the complete ridge from the toe near 6,600 ft or the upper ridge from the notch above the Stuart Glacier. Reckon on roughly eight or nine pitches of ridge above the notch, and considerably more from the toe.

What this entry is for is the decision made at its base, because the Gendarme is the one place on the ridge where there is a real choice and where a party that has not decided in advance loses time at 9,000 ft.

Both options are established. The tower goes in two pitches — a lieback, then the offwidth — and it can also be turned on ledges to the west, which is what the original 1956 ascent did and what most parties still do. The bypass is not an escape hatch invented by tired climbers; it is the older line.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARE AT THE BASE WHEN THE RIDGE STOPS BEING SCRAMBLING AND STANDS UP IN FRONT OF YOU. Everything below is fourth to mid-fifth class on excellent granite that you have been moving together on. The Gendarme is where that ends: a steep tower blocking the crest, roughly 500 ft below the summit, and there is nothing else on the ridge it can be confused with.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS WHETHER YOU CAN WALK ROUND IT. If a line of ledges leads off left (west) and lets you keep moving without roping up properly, you are at the bypass — the same place, and the decision point. If you are looking straight up at a clean lieback flake with an offwidth above it, you are at the climb.

SO THE TEST IN FOG IS A NEGATIVE ONE, and it is worth stating because parties do get this wrong on the way to the summit: if you are still on the ridge and have not yet had to make that choice, the Gendarme is ahead of you and the summit is not. If you have made it and are back on blocky fourth and low-fifth ground, the Gendarme is behind you and the summit is close.

A useful sanity check on the two pitches themselves: the second one has a reputation far worse than the climbing, and parties consistently report it going on good holds and jams with fixed gear in it. If the offwidth you are in feels desperate and unprotectable, look again at where you are — you may have entered the wrong crack on the tower.
hazards: Arriving at the tower late in the day with the summit still above and no quick way off the ridge
1,000+ ft of exposure on both sides of the crest
Rockfall from parties above on a popular ridge
Cold wind, and an unplanned bivy if the choice at the base costs too long
Retreat from above the Gendarme is awkward in either direction

approach_variants.name: Mountaineer Creek to the basin, then west onto the Stuart Glacier
approach_variants.season: Best while the couloir holds continuous snow and the steps take ice, roughly late spring into early summer; later the steps go rocky and the climbing turns mixed
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, follow the trail about three miles to the Colchuck Lake turnoff and continue past it for roughly another mile. Where the Stuart Lake trail switchbacks up and to the right, veer LEFT to stay in the main valley — the same leaving point every north-side route on this mountain uses.

Follow the valley about a mile and a half to where it steepens, then turn right and work up the steep slope into the small hanging valley above, the flat basin under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers at roughly 5,400 ft. Standard camp is here.

From the basin the route continues WEST, round the far side of the North Ridge, onto the Stuart Glacier. Entry to the couloir is at about 7,800 ft.

The couloir itself runs 40-50 degree snow, narrows to a short steep step whose character depends entirely on the season, then a second shorter step, then opens into a wider snowfield leading to a notch in the West Ridge. Six pitches of mixed ground follow from that notch to the summit.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE NORTH RIDGE ROCK RIB DECIDES IT, AND THE SIDE IT IS ON IS THE ANSWER. From the basin you are looking at four things in a row: the Sherpa Glacier, the Ice Cliff Glacier, the enormous rock rib of the North Ridge, and beyond it the Stuart Glacier.

You want to be past the rib. So: if the North Ridge rib is on your LEFT (east) you are on the Stuart Glacier and correct. If it is still on your RIGHT you have not gone far enough west and are on the Ice Cliff side. That is the same test the Ice Cliff Glacier route uses, read in the opposite direction, and it is the reliable one in cloud because it does not depend on seeing the summit.

SECOND TEST — WHAT THE COULOIR LEADS TO. This couloir does not go to the summit. It goes to a notch in the WEST RIDGE, which is on the far side of the mountain from where you camped. If the line you are looking up appears to head for the top of the peak, you are looking at the wrong feature.

THIRD, THE SHAPE. Entry is at about 7,800 ft and the couloir NARROWS above you before it widens again — moderate snow, then a short steep step, then a second shorter one, then an open snowfield. A line that is uniformly wide with no steps is not this one.

And the negative test: no hanging ice cliff or serac band should be above you anywhere. If there is one, you are back on the Ice Cliff Glacier, on the wrong side of the rib.
hazards: Crevasses on the Stuart Glacier below the couloir
Rockfall and wet-snow avalanche in the couloir as the day warms
The steep steps turning to bare ice or dry-tooling ground later in the season
Six pitches of mixed climbing above the notch, on the far side of the mountain from camp
An unmarked, often snow-covered off-trail turn out of the Mountaineer Creek valley

approach_variants.name: Mountaineer Creek south fork to the basin under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Jul while the glacier still carries continuous snow; it is also the standard early-season DESCENT off the north side, which is when most parties are on it
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead, follow the Lake Stuart / Colchuck Lake trail past the fork and leave the maintained tread near the meadow at about 4,500 ft, heading southwest and following the south fork of Mountaineer Creek upstream.

After a couple of miles a steep talus and boulder slope leads into the hanging valley beneath Sherpa Peak. This is the standard camp for the whole north side, and the flat ground itself is the arrival cue.

The glacier has three parts and it is worth knowing them before you set off in the dark: a lower snowfield, the glacier proper, and a steeper couloir in its northwest corner. Parties rope for the short glacier section and take the rope off above it.

This is a compact two-day outing, and it is the line most parties descend after climbing the Ice Cliff Glacier — so if you meet people coming down it at midday they are probably finishing a different climb.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SHERPA IS THE ONE WITH NO ICE ABOVE IT, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE TEST. Standing in the basin facing the mountain, the three features run in this order from your left: Sherpa Glacier, then Ice Cliff Glacier, then the huge rock rib of the North Ridge.

So the Sherpa is the LEFTMOST — the easternmost — of the two glaciers, and it is the one with nothing hanging over it. The Ice Cliff, immediately to its right, carries an obvious hanging ice cliff and serac band partway up. If there is a serac above you, you are one glacier too far right.

TOUCH TEST, and it is the one that works when you cannot see: the ground under the Ice Cliff is frozen avalanche debris mixed with fallen glacier ice, set solid — a talus field made of ice. The Sherpa's toe is ordinary snow over ordinary moraine. Standing on rubble made of ice is direct evidence you have drifted right.

WHERE IT TAKES YOU, as a confirmation rather than a route description: the Sherpa tops out at a notch on Mount Stuart's upper NORTH RIDGE at roughly 7,600 ft, followed by a short scramble. It does not lead to the West Ridge — that is the Stuart Glacier Couloir, on the other side of the rock rib.

And the steep part is in the glacier's NORTHWEST corner, not up its middle. If the steepest ground you can see is straight above the centre of the snowfield, look again at which feature you are under.
hazards: Crevasses in the middle section of the glacier and an icefall at its toe
Wet-snow avalanche and rockfall onto the glacier as the day warms
Straying right into the Ice Cliff Glacier's serac fall zone in poor visibility
A steep, unmaintained talus climb into the hanging valley with no trail
Log crossings of Mountaineer Creek that move with the snowpack

approach_variants.name: Ice Cliff Glacier to the top of the ice, then four easy pitches to the pillar
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug. The ice cliff step is shorter and more amenable early and gets steeper and barer as the season runs on, so the rock and the ice want opposite conditions
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the Ice Cliff Glacier's approach, and everything said about that line applies here: from the Stuart Lake trailhead follow the trail past the Colchuck Lake junction, leave it where it turns uphill for Stuart Lake, cross Mountaineer Creek and follow the climbers' path in the valley bottom to the hanging basin under the glaciers. Moraine camps sit around 6,800-7,000 ft; the flat basin below at about 5,400 ft is the more common bivy.

From camp the route ropes up and climbs the Ice Cliff Glacier itself. That glacier is the objective hazard of the day, not the pillar: icefall, spindrift and crevasses. Parties keep left to stay out from under the falling ice and swing wide right around the biggest crevasses.

At the top of the glacier is the ice cliff step, anywhere from ten to well over a hundred feet of 50-70 degree snow and ice.

There is no water above the moraine — carry it or melt.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
COUNT THE PITCHES ABOVE THE ICE, BECAUSE THE PILLAR IS NOT VISIBLE FROM THE GLACIER. From the top of the ice cliff step it is FOUR easy pitches to the base of the pillar, at roughly 8,200-8,400 ft. If you have done one or two and are already looking at hard cracks, you are on the face rather than on the pillar.

WHAT THE PILLAR IS: a discrete steep feature on the northeast face above the icefall, and the thing that identifies it is that the climbing changes character completely. Four moderate pitches of ordinary alpine ground end, and the next pitch is an immediately steep hand crack that jogs right at its top and ends on a poor, small ledge. That handcrack is the entrance. If the ground above you keeps rambling at the same angle, you have not reached it.

THE SEQUENCE ABOVE CONFIRMS IT, and is worth carrying in your head because the first belay is a bad one and you will want to know you are committing to the right thing: steep hands, then a pitch that shuffles about ten feet LEFT off the belay to a thin crack and finger-jams through the crux out RIGHT, then perfect hands on steep dirty rock to the top of the pillar. Three pitches, no more.

AND THE HARD RULE ABOUT BEING HERE AT ALL: there is no reasonable way to reverse this. Downclimbing or rappelling back into the icefall is worse than finishing, so arriving at the base of the pillar is a commitment to going over the top. Make that decision at the bottom of the glacier, not here.
hazards: Icefall and serac collapse on the Ice Cliff Glacier — the route's principal danger
Crevasses and spindrift on the glacier
A steep ice cliff step whose height and hardness vary through the season
Large loose blocks near the top of the pillar
No retreat: reversing the route through the icefall is more dangerous than continuing over the summit
No water above the moraine camp

approach_variants.name: Longs Pass to Ingalls Creek, then the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, with July the usual month; late season the loose ground below the headwall gets worse rather than better
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Longs Pass trail up open pine and sage switchbacks to Longs Pass at roughly 6,200 ft. Stop here — this is the one place on the whole day where you can see the entire south side of the mountain at once, and five minutes spent picking out the headwall from the pass is worth an hour of guessing later.

Drop off the north side of the pass on the steep, eroded boot path to Ingalls Creek, cross it, and join the Ingalls Creek trail.

Then the key move: from where the Longs Pass trail meets Ingalls Creek, go WEST along the creek trail and take the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir. That clearing is the line of ascent.

Above the clearing it is sustained scree and choss up to a cirque at about 8,700 ft. The technical climbing — five pitches, never harder than 5.7, plus a lot of fourth and easy fifth — starts up the centre of the headwall from there.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CIRQUE IS THE ARRIVAL, AND IT IS UNMISTAKABLE EVEN IN CLOUD BECAUSE IT CLOSES AROUND YOU. You climb loose ground for a long time and then the walls come up on three sides — very steep cliffs at about 8,700 ft with the summit directly above. That enclosure is the cue. Scree that keeps going with open ground on both sides means you are still below it.

WHICH CLEARING, WHICH IS THE ACTUAL PROBLEM: from the Ingalls Creek trail, count west from where the Longs Pass trail came down to the creek. The correct line is the FIRST MAJOR CLEARING WEST of Ulrich's Couloir. Ulrich's is the big obvious gully; if you are ascending a defined gully rather than an open clearing, you are in Ulrich's itself and on a different route entirely. And if the clearing you picked is EAST of that point, you are heading for the Cascadian Couloir — the standard walk-up and the usual descent — which is easier ground and will not put you under a headwall.

CONFIRMATION AT THE BASE: the technical pitches start up the CENTRE of the headwall, and they top out very close to the true summit. Nothing on this route is harder than 5.7. If the ground in front of you looks harder than that, you have drifted to one side of the centre.

PREVIEW IT FROM LONGS PASS. This is the rare approach where the whole objective is visible from a trail junction two thirds of the way through the day, and a party that identifies the headwall and the correct clearing from the pass essentially cannot get this wrong afterwards.
hazards: Frequent rockfall in the cirque and on the headwall, made worse by other parties
Sustained loose scree and choss on the ascent to the cirque, with no trail
A steep eroded descent path off Longs Pass, hard on the knees in both directions
An Ingalls Creek crossing that is a genuine ford in early-season snowmelt
Early-season snow and ice in the cirque
Afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter above the clearing

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Lake to the amphitheatre between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Jul-early Sep, once the snow below the wall has gone down enough to reach the start by a short scramble and before autumn storms
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, follow the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass and past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then take the climbers' trail onto the talus shoulder below Stuart's West Ridge.

The wall these routes are on sits in the amphitheatre roughly MIDWAY BETWEEN STUART PASS AND GOAT PASS, rising about 1,000 ft out of the snow. It is known as the West Face Wall — worth saying plainly, because it faces west and some descriptions of the mountain's south side sweep it in with the south face, which sends parties looking on the wrong aspect.

Bivy sites are at Stuart Pass and at Goat Pass. Most parties camp at one of them and walk in to the wall in the morning.

The descent goes over the top: continue up the West Ridge to the summit, or take the main West Ridge gully down with scrambling and downclimbing, breaking right onto a large bench where a single-rope rappel gets you back toward the Stuart Pass bivies.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
WALK THE FOOT OF THE WALL UNTIL YOU FIND A SPLITTER YOU CAN PUT BOTH HANDS IN. The start is an obvious hand-and-finger splitter crack, and it does NOT begin at ground level — it starts on a small ledge about 15 to 25 feet above the snow or talus, reached by a short scramble. That gap between the ground and the first moves is the single best confirmation you are in the right place: a crack running all the way to the snow is not this one.

WHERE ON THE WALL: you are in the amphitheatre between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass, roughly halfway between them, under about 1,000 ft of rock. If you are still on either pass you have not arrived; if the wall has ended and you are back on open talus you have walked past it.

SHARED START, AND SAY IT OUT LOUD BEFORE YOU RACK UP: this route and the other two lines on this wall begin at the SAME crack and share the first four pitches. The differences are higher up, at the major ledge system splitting the wall — this route goes LEFT there where the original line continues right. So finding the base correctly does not settle which route you are on, and the choice has to be made deliberately at that ledge rather than followed.

WHAT TO EXPECT ABOVE, as confirmation you started right: two pitches of corners and arêtes to a bolted anchor, then a long horizontal traverse rightwards on the third pitch. If nothing on your third pitch traverses, you are not on this line.
hazards: Snow at the foot of the wall early in the season, making the short scramble to the start awkward
Long runouts between placements and hidden loose chockstones
A west-facing wall that gets full afternoon sun and afternoon weather
Topping out high on the West Ridge with a long descent still to do
An unplanned bivy is a real outcome; parties carry for it

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Lake to the West Face Wall — same base as the other two lines on the wall
approach_variants.season: Late summer into early September, before autumn storms; the headwall is the point of the route and it wants dry rock
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the approach for the other West Face Wall routes. From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead, the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass, past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then the climbers' trail onto the talus shoulder below the West Ridge and on to the amphitheatre between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass. Camp at either pass.

This line is a direct start and direct finish grafted onto the existing routes: it climbs the first four pitches of the original line, steps left onto the middle pitches of the direct, and then breaks out onto its own two-pitch finish up an overhanging headwall splitter.

Because of that, none of the decisions on this climb are made at the bottom. The base is shared; what makes it this route is a pair of choices at the ledge system and again below the headwall.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE SAME SPLITTER THE OTHER TWO ROUTES USE — a hand-and-finger crack starting on a small ledge 15 to 25 feet off the snow or talus, gained by a short scramble. There is no separate King Kong start to look for, and hunting for one is how parties waste an hour at first light.

SO THE REAL ARRIVAL TEST IS THE WALL, NOT THE ROUTE: you want the amphitheatre roughly midway between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass, with about 1,000 ft of rock rising straight out of the snow above you. Anywhere still on a pass, or anywhere the wall has petered out into talus, is wrong. And the aspect is WEST — this wall takes the afternoon sun, so if you are standing under a face that has been in shade all afternoon you are on the wrong side of the mountain.

WHERE THIS ROUTE ACTUALLY BECOMES ITSELF, which is what you have to know at the base because you cannot see it from there: four pitches up the original line, then LEFT onto the direct for two pitches, then the two-pitch finish. The connector out to the finish is a roof bulge and a stem-box on overhanging jugs; the headwall pitch above it is a splitter on a steeply overhanging wall with more than thirty metres of air under it and two fixed nuts at its top.

IF YOU REACH A LEDGE SYSTEM AND SIMPLY CONTINUE RIGHT, you are on the original line and will finish on it. Nothing will stop you or tell you. The decision is yours and it is made in the middle of the wall.
hazards: Significant runouts between protection placements
Loose rock with hidden chockstones
Thirty-plus metres of overhanging exposure on the headwall pitch, with retreat from it awkward
Alpine weather on a west-facing wall late in the season
An unplanned bivy is a documented outcome on this route

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the true-right margin of the Colchuck Glacier
approach_variants.season: Roughly Apr-Jun as a snow and ice climb; by high summer the entry moat opens and the couloir sheds rock
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, follow Stuart Lake Trail about two and a half miles to the signed junction and fork RIGHT for Colchuck Lake — straight on goes to Stuart Lake and a different valley. Switchback up to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, roughly four miles and 2,200 ft in, and fill water: it is the last easy source.

Take the boot path along the lake's EAST shore, which is faster than the west, to the inlet at the south end. Leave the trail there and climb talus, heather benches or snow up the basin to the toe of the Colchuck Glacier at roughly 6,600-6,800 ft.

Now the important part. Do NOT continue up-glacier toward the col — that is the Colchuck Glacier route. Traverse along the glacier's TRUE-RIGHT (climber's right) margin toward Colchuck Peak's north side, staying well right of the fall line under the face.

If Eightmile Road is gated in early season, add roughly four miles of road each way.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COULOIRS COME IN ORDER, AND COUNTING THEM IS THE TEST. Walking up the Colchuck Glacier along its true-right margin you pass features in a fixed sequence, and this one is the SECOND deep slot you meet, not the first.

Lowest on the glacier: the North Buttress Couloir. Above it, and starting with two rope-lengths of ice below a hidden couloir: the Holsten-Hilden. HIGHER UP THE GLACIER than either: the Northeast Couloir — the one you want. Above and south of it: the rock of the Northeast Buttress.

SO THE PAIRED CHECK IS SLOT-AND-RIB. You are correct when you are standing in an obvious narrow slot splitting the face, with the prominent rock buttress immediately to your SOUTH. If the buttress is not there, you are too low on the glacier. If you are scrambling onto the toe of that rock rather than into a slot, you are on the Northeast Buttress and on a fourteen-pitch rock route instead of a snow and ice one.

THE MOAT IS PART OF THE ARRIVAL, not an obstacle before it: gaining the couloir means crossing the moat at the glacier's edge, and it runs from a step-across in early season to an awkward downclimb by late summer. If you reach rock with no moat to cross at all, you have probably reached it somewhere it is filled and should confirm the slot above you before committing.

WHAT IT DOES ABOVE, as confirmation: the couloir winds up, steepens, and runs into a steep WALL. The exit is along the base of that wall to the climber's LEFT, finishing on 60-plus degree snow or ice to the summit ridge. A couloir that simply keeps going without hitting a wall is not this one.
hazards: Rockfall down the couloir once the sun reaches the face
An entry moat that can require an awkward downclimb by mid-to-late summer
Avalanche-prone slopes above Colchuck Lake in spring and early summer
Steep snow and ice to 60-plus degrees at the exit
Reversing the couloir is discouraged — plan on the Colchuck Glacier walk-off, which is long

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the glacier's true-right margin to the lowest point of the buttress
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep for the rock; the moat crossing is easiest early and hardest in a lean year late
approach_variants.notes:
As for the Colchuck Glacier route: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail two and a half miles to the signed fork, right onto the Colchuck Lake Trail and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about four miles and 2,200 ft, and the last reliable water on the route.

Follow the east-shore boot path to the inlet at the south end, then climb talus and snow up the basin to the toe of the Colchuck Glacier at roughly 6,600-6,800 ft. Instead of continuing toward the col, angle up and across the glacier's true-right margin toward the peak's northeast side.

Cross the moat where snow meets rock — a snow bridge or a wedged block in a good year, and the technical crux of the approach in a lean one. Parties do rope for this.

Given fourteen-plus pitches and a multi-stage approach, most parties either start well before dawn from the car or camp at Colchuck Lake and climb from there. There is no water above the lake.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BUTTRESS IS THE ROCK JUST SOUTH OF THE COULOIR, AND THE COULOIR IS THE THING YOU LOOK FOR FIRST. It is easier to identify a deep slot in a face than a rib on it, so use the Northeast Couloir as your marker and then step south onto the rock beside it. If you are in a narrow snow slot, you are one feature too far north.

ARRIVAL IS THE LOWEST POINT OF THE ROCK. The commonly climbed start gains the buttress at its lowest point and heads for wide, broken cracks at about 5.8. Standing at the right place there is nothing lower to climb — the rock runs down into the glacier and the moat, and you had to cross that moat to reach it.

TWO STARTS EXIST, AND MIXING THEM IS THE ROUTINE ERROR HERE. There is the more travelled version described above and an older, separate start; they do not meet until around the fifth pitch. So a party that steps onto rock wherever the moat happened to be crossable can find itself on neither, on unfamiliar ground, with no way to tell. Cross the moat where it puts you at the LOWEST rock, not where it is most convenient.

CONFIRMATION IN THE FIRST TWO PITCHES: wide, broken cracks on generally solid rock leading to the crest below a large headwall, then a downclimb of about fifteen feet off the crest before ramps take you up and right. A start with no downclimb in the first few pitches is not this line.

AND THE BAIL-OUT WARNING: this route has a real reputation for parties retreating because they cannot find the crux dihedral higher up. If the base was ambiguous, the rest of the day will be worse.
hazards: A moat crossing that can be the technical crux of the day in a lean snow year
Two established starts that do not converge until around pitch five
Inconsistent rock — clean crack pitches interspersed with loose, mossy and lichened ground
Loose debris on the long rising ledge traverse, onto anyone below
No water above Colchuck Lake
A long walk-off down the Colchuck Glacier after a fourteen-pitch day

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the glacier to the ice below the Hidden Couloir
approach_variants.season: Winter and early spring, when the two ice pitches at the base are formed; the first ascent was in January
approach_variants.notes:
As for the other north-side lines: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail to the signed fork, right for Colchuck Lake and up the switchbacks to the lake at 5,570 ft, then the east-shore path to the inlet and up the basin to the Colchuck Glacier and moraine below the peak's northeast face.

In the season this route is in, expect the road to be gated well below the trailhead and the approach to be a longer day than the summer figures suggest. No trailhead-to-base time is given here because the published accounts are winter ones and vary too much to average.

Above the base the route runs two 60 m pitches of ice, several hundred feet of 50-60 degree snow trending up and left, then unconsolidated snow over rock, a short leftward traverse into a chimney at about M6, and a final steep band to a notch on the north ridge crest.

A documented variation climbs the ice start and then continues up the Hidden Couloir itself and across the North Buttress — a more sustained moderate line and a genuinely different day.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE HIDDEN COULOIR IS THE MARKER AND THE ROUTE STARTS UNDERNEATH IT. This is the cleanest base identification on the whole face: find the Hidden Couloir, and the start is immediately BELOW it — two 60 m pitches of good ice leading up to its base.

POSITION ON THE GLACIER, which is how you find the couloir in the first place: this line sits BETWEEN the North Buttress Couloir and the Northeast Couloir. So walking up the glacier you pass the North Buttress Couloir first; the next thing is this. If you have already passed a second deep slot you have gone too high and are under the Northeast Couloir.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS THE ICE ITSELF. This is the only line on the face that begins with two full rope-lengths of continuous ice off the deck. If the ground in front of you is snow, or mixed, or rock, it is not the start — whatever else it might be.

AND THE DIVERGENCE ABOVE, because it is decided a couple of pitches up and not at the bottom: from the top of the ice this route goes UP AND LEFT from the base of the Hidden Couloir onto difficult mixed ground. The variation instead climbs INTO the Hidden Couloir. Both start on the same ice. One is M6; the other is sustained moderate. Know which you have come for before you leave the second belay.

If you cannot find a couloir above your ice, you are not below the Hidden Couloir and should not assume the ice is the right ice.
hazards: A winter approach with the road gated, in avalanche terrain above Colchuck Lake
Two rope-lengths of AI3 ice off the deck with committing ground above
Unconsolidated snow over rock above the ice — poor protection
An M6 chimney reached by a short traverse, with retreat from it difficult
Short winter daylight on a Grade IV route
Topping out on the north ridge crest, still a long way from the ordinary descent

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the Colchuck Glacier to the col, then the ridge west to the summit
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep as a scramble; earlier the glacier is a snow climb and wants an axe and crampons
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead at 3,400 ft, follow the Stuart Lake Trail about two and a half miles to the signed junction, fork right and switchback up to Colchuck Lake at about 5,570 ft — roughly four miles and 2,200 ft.

Follow the boot path round the lake and across the boulder field at its south end into the basin, then climb the Colchuck Glacier toward the col between Colchuck Peak and Dragontail. Keep climber's right on the glacier to reduce exposure to rockfall coming off Dragontail's north face.

From the col the route is the ridge running WEST to Colchuck's summit — Class 2-3, hands needed in places, no protection, generally solid granite with good friction.

Be aware that this route's stored approach text in this catalog says to traverse NORTHEAST from the lake to reach the ridge base. That is the wrong direction: the peak lies south-west of the lake and the col lies south-east of the summit. Navigate from the glacier and the col, not from that sentence.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL IS THE BASE, AND YOU KNOW YOU ARE ON IT BECAUSE THE GROUND FALLS AWAY BEHIND YOU. Walking up the Colchuck Glacier you are in a closed basin; at the col the far side opens and drops south into the Ingalls Creek drainage. That change from enclosed to open is the arrival, and it happens whether or not you can see anything.

THEN TURN RIGHT. From the col, Colchuck Peak is WEST and Dragontail is EAST. The two peaks share this col, so a party that gains it in cloud and turns the wrong way is climbing a different mountain on a different route — and Dragontail's side of the col is not Class 2-3.

THE HANDS TEST: this ridge is Class 2-3. You will use your hands in places, and you should never need protection or a rope. If you find yourself on ground where you want gear, you have left the crest onto the north or south flank, and the correct answer is to come back to the crest rather than to press on.

CONFIRMATION UNDERFOOT: the granite here is solid with good friction, unlike the loose scree of the glacier basin below. Rambling on loose rubble means you are still below the ridge proper.

A WARNING WORTH CARRYING: this is also the standard DESCENT for the harder routes on the peak's north side, so parties will be coming down it. Meeting people descending is not evidence you are on the wrong line — it is evidence you are on the right one.
hazards: Rockfall onto the Colchuck Glacier from Dragontail's north face — stay climber's right
Crevasses and a soft afternoon snow surface on the glacier
Exposure on the ridge crest despite the easy grade
Wandering off the crest onto steeper flanking ground in poor visibility
Afternoon thunderstorms on an exposed ridge with no shelter

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core Enchantments to the middle of the south face
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once Aasgard Pass is clear of the snow that bridges the creek beneath it
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail two and a half miles to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. Boulder-hop the east shore to the boulder field at the south end, then climb Aasgard Pass — about 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of steep loose scree, the physical crux of the approach. Into early July, snow can bridge a hidden creek and moat on the left side of the gully; that hazard has caused serious injuries and at least one death.

From the pass at about 7,800 ft, drop gently into the upper Core basin and travel cross-country north over slabs and heather past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn, the usual bivy. The base of the south face is roughly fifteen to twenty minutes from there.

Overnight camping in the Core Zone needs a permit, so many parties do the whole thing in one long day instead.

When Aasgard or this trailhead is closed, the Snow Lakes trail is the longer alternative, reaching the same face past Lake Viviane.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS IS THE ROUTE IN THE MIDDLE, AND THAT IS THE FIRST AND MOST USEFUL FACT. Walking along the foot of the south face, the start sits at about the MIDDLE of the base. The lines on the left flank of the face all top out on the West Ridge; this one is the classic that goes to the actual summit.

THE FEATURE TEST: you are looking for a chimney system on steep white granite. Pitch one takes either a 5.6/5.7 chimney or a wide crack immediately LEFT of that chimney, and lands on low fifth-class ground with trees on it. Trees at the top of your first pitch is a good confirmation.

HOW TO TELL IT FROM ITS TWO NEIGHBOURS, which is the actual problem on this face because three routes start within a hundred feet of each other:
  - If you can see TWO PROMINENT V-SHAPES on the face and you are at a chimney to the LEFT of them, you are at Beckey-Davis — one route too far RIGHT.
  - If you are about fifty feet LEFT of where you think the standard line is, you are at Der Sportsman, and its first pitch is 5.11+ rather than 5.7. A first pitch that feels desperate is the loudest possible signal you are on the wrong route.

STARTING COORDINATE, published for pitch one: roughly 47.48681, -120.78457. In fog with a GPS that is decisive; on a clear day the shape of the face is better.

AND THE ARRIVAL CONFIRMATION HIGHER UP: pitch five squeezes between a chockstone into a flaring chimney, and pitch six is a left-facing corner to the SUMMIT. If your route runs out on the West Ridge instead of the summit, you are on one of the left-flank lines.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose steep scree, and a hidden creek and moat under snow into early July with a fatal history
Avalanche on the pass in shoulder season
Unmarked cross-country travel over slabs and talus for the last stretch, with no tread
A flaring squeeze chimney at mid-height that is awkward with a pack
A shared north-side rappel descent that gets congested when several parties are on the face
Snafflehounds at the base and at bivy sites will chew boots and gear left out

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core to the chimney left of the two Vs
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
The Core Enchantments approach, shared with every other line on this face: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, then the boulder field at the south end and Aasgard Pass — 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of loose scree, hazardous under lingering snow into early July because of a creek and moat hidden beneath it.

From the pass, cross-country north past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn and the base of the south face, roughly 7.5 to 8 miles and 4,600 ft one way.

If the standard trailhead or the pass is shut — wildfire closures have done this — the Snow Lakes trail reaches the same face by a longer and less direct line past Lake Viviane and a climbers' path onto the south side of the peak. One party clocked that version at about ten miles and 6,000 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LOOK FOR TWO LARGE Vs AND START IN THE CHIMNEY TO THEIR LEFT. That is the whole identification, it is published in exactly those terms, and the accompanying note is that you cannot miss it. Two prominent V-shaped features on the south face; the route's first pitch takes the chimney immediately LEFT of them.

CONFIRM WITH THE FIRST PITCH ITSELF: from the chimney you move LEFT and climb up on knobs to a belay, at about 5.7. Knobs after a leftward move out of a chimney is the signature. If you are pulling straight up out of the chimney with no traverse, look again.

POSITION RELATIVE TO ITS NEIGHBOUR, which is the check that catches the common error: this route is to the climber's RIGHT of the classic south-face line. So if you are at the middle of the base of the face, you are one route too far left. Walk RIGHT until the two Vs are on your right-hand side and you are at a chimney.

AND A DISTANCE CHECK ON THE ROUTE AS A WHOLE: seven pitches, about 650 ft, running 5.5 to 5.9, with a long chimney-gully crossing to a big ledge partway up and a forced rightward dihedral as the crux. A four- or five-pitch route ending on the West Ridge is one of the shorter lines on the left flank, not this.

IN CLOUD, when you cannot see the Vs from a distance, walk the foot of the face and count chimneys rather than guessing: the Vs are large features and they are visible from close under them even when the summit is not.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose scree, and a hidden creek and moat under snow into early July
Avalanche on the pass in shoulder season
Unmarked cross-country travel for the final approach
Six rappels down the north face on ageing natural anchors — carry extra tat
A possible extra rappel from the West Ridge notch to regain the south-face base
Snafflehounds at the base will eat gear left unattended

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core to the left flank of the south face
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
As for the rest of the face: Stuart Lake trailhead at about 3,600 ft, Stuart Lake Trail two and a half miles to the signed Colchuck Lake Trail junction, right and across Mountaineer Creek — a rock-hop or log crossing, and the last easy water for a while — then 1.6 miles of switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft.

Boulder-hop the east shore to the boulder field at the south end, then Aasgard Pass: 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of steep loose dirt and scree, cairned when snow-free. In early season, and often into July, snow bridges a hidden creek and moat on the left side of the gully; people have been badly hurt and killed there postholing or glissading into it.

From the pass at 7,841 ft, drop into the upper Core past Isolation and Tranquil Lake and continue cross-country a mile or so north over slabs and heather benches toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn. The start is fifteen to twenty minutes from a Gnome Tarn camp.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
GO TO THE OUTSIDE CORNER AND START JUST RIGHT OF IT. The left flank of the south face ends in an outside corner — the arête where the south face turns the corner onto the west side — and this route begins just to the RIGHT of it, on a right-leaning crack system leading to a stembox.

THAT CORNER IS THE ANCHOR FOR THE WHOLE LEFT END OF THE FACE, and the three routes here are placed off it:
  - Left of the corner, on the west face proper: a line with a large roof at its base, sometimes called the Elephant Ear.
  - Just right of the corner: this route.
  - About 100 ft further right: another four-pitch line to the West Ridge.
So if you are under a roof, you have gone one route too far left; if you have walked a hundred feet right of the corner, one too far right.

THE HONEST WARNING ABOUT WHERE THIS ROUTE ENDS, because it is the best single check that you are on the left flank at all: this line and its immediate neighbours top out on the WEST RIDGE, not on the summit. Only the classic line at the middle of the face reaches the true summit. If you have come for the summit and started here, you have an extra scramble at the top and you started on the wrong route.

SEQUENCE CHECK: right-leaning cracks to a stembox, then a roof and hand-crack pitch, then slabby and wide ground past a chimney with loose rock, then a final splitter corner. Five pitches, about 450 ft. A seven-pitch line with two big V-features low down is Beckey-Davis, well to your right.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose steep scree, and a hidden creek and moat under snow into early July with a fatal history
Avalanche on the pass in shoulder season
Loose rock past the chimney at mid-height
Natural, non-bolted rappel anchors on the north side shared with several routes; inspect and back up old tat
Cross-country navigation over slabs with no tread for the last mile
Core Zone camping requires a permit that most parties do not have

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, then a hundred feet right of the left-flank classic
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
The shared Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, then the boulder field at the south end and Aasgard Pass — 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of loose scree, the crux of the walk in, dangerous under snow into early July and avalanche-prone in shoulder season.

From the pass, cross-country north past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn and the base of the south face — roughly 7.5 to 8 miles and 4,600 ft one way, the last stretch unmarked over slabs and talus.

Four pitches, about 450 ft: a short crack and slab to a corner, a long exposed and somewhat dirty face-crack pitch, a corner with a bouldery move, and a finishing fingers-to-hands pitch to the ridge.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
PACE IT OFF FROM THE LEFT-FLANK CLASSIC: this route starts ABOUT 100 FEET TO THE RIGHT of it, on the west side of the south face. That is a measurable distance rather than a description, and it is the reason this entry is worth having — everything else on this end of the face is identified relative to the same outside corner.

SO THE PROCEDURE IN POOR VISIBILITY IS TWO STEPS. First find the outside corner where the south face turns onto the west side. The classic left-flank line starts just right of that corner. Then walk right roughly a hundred feet along the base. That is where you are.

WHAT TELLS YOU YOU HAVE OVERSHOT: keep walking right along the base and the ground under the middle of the face is where the summit route starts, and beyond that the two large V-features of the next line along. Reaching either means you have gone several hundred feet too far.

WHAT TELLS YOU YOU ARE SHORT: a large roof at the base means you have crossed the corner onto the west face entirely and are two routes left.

FIRST-PITCH CONFIRMATION: a SHORT crack and slab leading to a corner. It is not a long lead and it is not hard. The long, exposed, somewhat dirty face crack is the SECOND pitch. If your first pitch is long and dirty you have started one pitch too high or on the wrong line.

AND THE TOP-OUT CHECK: this route finishes on the West Ridge, not the summit — the same as its two neighbours on this flank. That shared finish is why they share one rappel descent on the north side.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose scree with a hidden creek and moat under early-season snow
A long, exposed and dirty second pitch
Natural non-bolted rappel anchors on the north side, periodically rebuilt as old tat accumulates
Unmarked cross-country approach over slabs and talus
Afternoon thunderstorms with a long walk back over the pass

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, round the corner onto the west face
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. This one faces west rather than south, so it comes into the sun later in the day and is a cold morning start
approach_variants.notes:
The shared Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, the boulder field at the south end, and Aasgard Pass — 2,000 ft of loose scree in 1.25 miles, hazardous under snow into early July.

From the pass, cross-country north past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn, roughly 7.5 to 8 miles and 4,600 ft one way from the trailhead.

Five pitches, about 450 ft: a burly and somewhat dirty roof pitch straight off the deck, an exposed corner to a good ledge, a short aid section through steep ground, a fingery crack between two features, and then the final corner crack shared with the neighbouring line to finish.

Because it joins that neighbour near the top, it shares its descent: a single full-length rappel on the north side and about thirty minutes of scrambling back round to the base.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROOF AT GROUND LEVEL IS THE MARKER, AND IT IS THE ONLY ONE YOU NEED. This route starts underneath a large roof formation at the very base — climbing it is the first pitch, straight off the deck. No other line at this end of the peak starts under a roof. Standing under a big overhang means you are here.

WHICH SIDE OF THE CORNER YOU ARE ON DECIDES IT. The south face turns an outside corner onto the west side. This route is LEFT of that corner, i.e. on the WEST face; the left-flank south-face classic is just RIGHT of it. So: corner on your right, roof over your head, west face — correct. Corner on your left and no roof — you have stepped back onto the south face and are on a different climb.

ASPECT AS A SANITY CHECK: this one faces WEST. If you have been standing in the sun all morning, you are on the south face and not here.

MID-ROUTE CONFIRMATION: there is a pair of rock features partway up that the route is named for, with a steep fingery crack running between them. If you never pass between two distinct features, you are not on this line.

AND THE TOP: this route joins its neighbour's final corner crack, so the last pitch is shared and the summit is not reached directly — you finish on the West Ridge. That shared finish is also why the rappel descent is the same one.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose scree with a hidden creek and moat under early-season snow
A burly, dirty roof pitch immediately off the ground
A short aid section through steep terrain at mid-height
Shared natural rappel anchors on the north side that have been rebuilt and relocated over the years
A west aspect: late sun, cold mornings, and afternoon weather arriving unseen from behind the peak

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, fifty feet left of the standard south-face line
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the route is a hard rock climb and wants dry, warm granite
approach_variants.notes:
The Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail 2.5 miles to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. From the boulder field at the lake's south end, Aasgard Pass — 1.25 miles gaining about 2,000 ft of steep loose scree and dirt, the physical crux of the approach, with a hidden creek and moat under lingering snow into early July.

From the pass at 7,841 ft, continue cross-country through the upper Core past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn. Parties commonly bivy at the tarn, about twenty minutes from the base. There is no maintained trail for the last stretch.

The Snow Lakes trail is the longer alternative when Aasgard or the trailhead is closed: past Nada and Snow Lakes to Lake Viviane, then up and right toward Temple Lake and up climbers' paths through boulders to the base of the south face.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FIFTY FEET LEFT OF THE STANDARD SOUTH FACE ROUTE. That is the published position and it is a pace count, not a description — find the classic line at the middle of the base of the face, then walk left about fifty feet.

THE FIRST PITCH IS THE CHECK, AND IT IS A BRUTAL ONE. This route's opening pitch is 5.11+. The line fifty feet to your right opens at 5.6 or 5.7 in a chimney. There is no ambiguity between those two pieces of climbing: if you are cruising your first pitch, you are on the wrong route, and if you are fighting a tipsy crux entering a stembox, you are on this one.

WHAT THE FIRST PITCH LOOKS LIKE FROM THE GROUND, so you can commit before you leave the deck: an easy, unappealing LEFT-SLANTING crack system leading up to a stance below an obvious stembox. The unremarkable start is deceptive and is exactly why the fifty-foot offset matters — the interesting rock is not visible from the base.

BELAY CONFIRMATION: pitch one ends at a TWO-BOLT ANCHOR after liebacking and stemming up the right of twin cracks. Most of this face is natural gear; arriving at bolts is strong evidence you are on this line rather than on a neighbour.

AND THE NAMED PITCH HIGHER UP: an undercling flake pitch that parties call the money pitch, then a committing corner where the route switches cracks. If you never leave one crack for another, you have wandered onto adjoining ground.

DESCENT NOTE THAT AFFECTS THE APPROACH DECISION: this one rappels the north side in five, then needs one more rappel from the balanced-rock landmark at the base of the West Ridge to get back down to your packs.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose steep scree with a hidden creek and moat under early-season snow, and a fatal history
A 5.11+ crux on the first pitch, so retreat decisions come early
A loose block in the finishing chimney
Mixed rappel anchors on the north side — one bolted station near the top, gear and slung naturals below
Unmarked cross-country approach over slabs and talus
Core Zone camping needs a permit

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass, then southwest across the Upper Enchantments to the col below the tower
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; earlier the traverse from the pass is a snow crossing and the col wants an axe
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead at about 3,400 ft, follow the Stuart Lake Trail south along Mountaineer Creek; at about 2.5 miles bear left at the signed junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail. Cross Mountaineer Creek on logs and boulders — an awkward wet ford in early-season high water — and climb through forest and a boulder field to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, roughly four miles in. Last reliable water.

Take the climbers' path along the lake's east and south shore through talus to the foot of Aasgard Pass, then up the eroded boot track: roughly 2,200 ft in well under a mile of loose scree and blocks, holding snow and ice into July.

From the pass at about 7,800 ft, work south to southwest across talus — initially as though heading for the snow route on Dragontail's east side — toward the tower, then up snow or Class 2 rock to the col just SOUTHWEST of it.

Figure six and a half to seven miles one way with something like 4,700-4,900 ft of gain.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL SOUTHWEST OF THE TOWER IS THE BASE, AND THE TOWER ITSELF IS THE LANDMARK — a distinct rock pinnacle standing alone at the west end of the Enchantments, dividing the upper basin between Little Annapurna and Dragontail. It is a pinnacle, not a summit on a ridge, so once you are close enough to see anything at all it is unambiguous.

WHICH SIDE OF IT YOU WANT: the SOUTHWEST col. From the col the climbing goes up a sharp ridge for about 100 ft and then traverses a few feet RIGHT onto the south face. If the ground above your col does not narrow into a sharp ridge within the first hundred feet, you are at the wrong notch.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE OTHER ROUTES, and it is a clean one because the two cols are on opposite sides:
  - Snow or Class 2 rock up to a col, sharp ridge above, traverse right onto the south face — this route.
  - A col with a STEEP SNOWFIELD to cross before you reach rock — that is the west-side line, and the snowfield is the tell.
  - Working EAST or SOUTHEAST from the pass toward light-coloured rock below Dragontail's south ridge, with no col involved at all — that is the east face line.

ARRIVAL CONFIRMED BY THE SUMMIT ITSELF: the top of this tower is guarded by a four-foot slot you have to jump. If you have scrambled to a high point and there was no slot, you are on a subsidiary block and not on the tower.

GRADE CHECK: the hardest single move on this line is one 5.5 step-up after the Class 4 traverse. Ground that feels harder than that means you missed the traverse right and are climbing the face direct.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: 2,200 ft of loose eroded scree with rockfall from parties above, holding snow into July
Serious exposure on the final approach scramble to the col
A four-foot slot that must be jumped to reach the true summit, with real consequence
Fast-building afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter in the Upper Enchantments
Protection on the 5.5 step can be hard to find
The downclimb off the south face is the crux for most parties

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass to the same southwest col, taking the corner rather than the face traverse
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the south face approach as far as the col: Stuart Lake trailhead to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, the boot path round the lake's east and south shore, Aasgard Pass at about 7,800 ft, then south across talus toward the tower and up snow or Class 2 rock to the col just southwest of it.

Published figures for the day put it at roughly six to eight hours and about 4,200 ft of gain from the trailhead to this point, which is a wide enough spread that it should be treated as a range rather than a plan.

From the col the climbing is short: about 100 ft up the sharp ridge, a few feet right onto the south face at Class 4, a 5.5 step-up, a short face, and a scramble to the summit slot.

What separates this entry from the south face one is not where you stand but what you do from there, so the useful content is in the base finding rather than in the walk.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
SAME COL, DIFFERENT FIRST MOVE — AND YOU SHOULD KNOW WHICH YOU ARE DOING BEFORE YOU LEAVE THE COL. From the col southwest of the tower, this line goes straight up the SHARP RIDGE ABOVE THE COL for about 100 ft. That ridge crest is the route. The south face line uses the same ground and then commits to the traverse right; both converge at the same Class 4 step and 5.5 move.

SO THE ARRIVAL TEST IS THE COL, and it has three parts:
  1. You reached it by ascending SNOW or CLASS 2 ROCK from the basin — not by crossing a steep snowfield, which is the west-side approach, and not by traversing across light rock under Dragontail's south ridge, which is the east face.
  2. Above you the ground rises as a defined, narrow crest rather than as an open face.
  3. The tower's summit block is directly above that crest, with the four-foot summit slot the last obstacle.

IF THE CREST FEELS WRONG: the ridge is sharp and exposed, and the recorded warning about this line is that placements on the crux are tricky to find. That is a route-finding statement as much as a protection one — a leader who cannot find gear may be a few feet off the correct line, on ground with fewer features.

AND THE COMMON MISTAKE: parties heading for the tower from Aasgard Pass drift too far EAST, toward Dragontail. If Dragontail's bulk is directly ahead of you rather than off to your right, you have gone past the tower.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose steep scree, snow into July
Exposure on the sharp ridge above the col
Hard-to-find protection on the 5.5 crux
A four-foot summit slot that must be jumped
Afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter
Downclimbing the south face back to the col is the usual descent and is Class 2-3 with one harder step

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass to the col, then a steep snowfield crossing onto the west side
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The snowfield is the point of this variant and it is present through most of the usable season — carry an axe regardless of the date
approach_variants.notes:
As for the other routes on the tower: Stuart Lake trailhead, the Colchuck Lake Trail to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, the boot path round the lake, and Aasgard Pass at about 7,800 ft. Then south across the basin to the col behind the tower.

What is different here is the last few hundred feet. From the col a STEEP SNOWFIELD has to be crossed to reach the base of the buttress on the west side. An ice axe is the standard recommendation, and parties downclimb it in self-arrest position on the way out, which tells you the angle.

The climbing above is mostly Class 4 on solid granite with good holds, a short Class 5 chimney partway up, and a friction section to finish. Two pitches.

The descent combines rappelling and downclimbing, including an exposed ledge traverse, back to the col — so the snowfield gets crossed twice.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SNOWFIELD IS THE ROUTE MARKER, AND IT IS THE CLEANEST ONE ON THE WHOLE TOWER. Of the tower's routes, this is the only one where the base is reached by crossing steep snow after the col. So: if you left the col and immediately started climbing rock, you are on one of the other lines. If you left the col, crossed a steep snowfield, and are now standing under rock on the WEST side, you are here.

CARRY THAT AS A DECISION, NOT AN OBSERVATION. Arriving at the col without an axe means this route is off the table for the day, and that is a judgement to make at Colchuck Lake rather than at 8,400 ft.

CONFIRMATION FROM THE ROCK: the buttress here is solid granite with good natural hand and footholds and it goes mostly at Class 4, with one short Class 5 CHIMNEY partway up and a friction face to finish. The other routes on the tower are characterised by a sharp ridge above the col and a traverse onto the south face; neither has a chimney. A chimney at mid-height is positive evidence you are on the west buttress.

ORIENTATION CHECK IN CLOUD: from the base you are on the far side of the tower from the Upper Enchantment lakes basin you walked in through. If the lakes are still below and behind you, you have not crossed to the west side.

AND THE DESCENT MATTERS TO THE ARRIVAL DECISION: the way down involves an exposed ledge traverse and rappels back to the col, then the snowfield again in self-arrest position. This is the tower's most committing line and the base is where you commit.
hazards: A steep snowfield crossing to reach the base, and again in descent — ice axe essential
Aasgard Pass: loose steep scree, snow into July
An exposed ledge traverse on the descent
A short Class 5 chimney mid-route with a pack
Afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter and a snow crossing between you and the way out

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass, then east and southeast to the light-coloured rock below Dragontail's south ridge
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep once the talus is clear; snow patches persist right up to the base into midsummer
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead at about 3,400 ft, the Stuart Lake Trail to the signed fork at about 2.5 miles, left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail and across Mountaineer Creek, then up through forest and a boulder field to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, roughly 4.3 miles. Last reliable water.

Skirt the lake's east and south shore on climbers' trail through talus to the foot of Aasgard Pass, then up the eroded boot path — 2,200 to 2,500 ft in well under a mile of loose scree, boulders and lingering snow. This is the biggest hazard of the day and the place route-finding errors happen in cloud.

From the pass at roughly 7,750-7,800 ft, the split from the other Witches Tower routes happens immediately. Instead of contouring west toward the col used by the south face and southwest corner lines, work EAST and SOUTHEAST across talus and boulders below Dragontail's south ridge, staying high along the rim of the basin, to reach the tower's east-facing side.

No water above Colchuck Lake beyond snowmelt trickles.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU NEVER GO TO A COL ON THIS ONE, AND THAT IS THE TEST. Every other route on the tower is reached by gaining a notch — the southwest col, or the col behind the tower. This line approaches the EAST side directly across talus, staying high along the rim of the basin under Dragontail's south ridge. If you find yourself climbing to a notch, you are on a different route.

WHICH DIRECTION FROM THE PASS: east to southeast. The col routes go west and southwest. That is a genuine fork at the top of Aasgard Pass and it is made within a few minutes of arriving there, so decide before you top out rather than after.

THE ROCK IS THE MARKER: aim for the light-coloured, white granite face on the tower's east side. From below it, the route works up a series of ZIG-ZAGGING LEDGES to the summit — that stepped, ledgy character is what identifies it. A face that is continuous and blank in front of you is not the line, and there is a well-known short hand crack on one of the standard variations through it.

GRADE CHECK: this is fourth class, one pitch, with little or no protection typically placed. If you are looking at sustained fifth-class climbing you have picked the wrong start on the face.

AND THE SUMMIT CHECK COMMON TO THE WHOLE TOWER: the true summit is guarded by a four-foot slot that has to be jumped. No slot means no summit.

HONEST LIMIT ON THIS ENTRY: the east side of the tower is less documented than the col routes, and published descriptions of the exact start line are thin. The direction from the pass, the white rock and the zig-zag ledges are solid; a precise first-move marker is not available and none is invented here.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: 2,200-2,500 ft of loose eroded scree, snow and ice into July, rockfall from parties above
Blocky talus and short snow patches right up to the base
Little or no protection on the climbing itself
A four-foot summit slot that must be jumped
The descent is normally down the south face or southwest corner, i.e. NOT the way you came — you finish on the other side of the tower
No water above Colchuck Lake

approach_variants.name: Mountaineer Creek to the Sherpa-Argonaut basin, then talus west-northwest to the lower notch
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep once the talus is clear; the basin holds snow into early summer
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead on Eightmile Road, follow the Stuart Lake Trail along Mountaineer Creek for roughly three and a half to four miles. Before the lakes, leave the maintained trail, cross Mountaineer Creek, and pick up a boot path and cairns climbing talus benches on the slope west of the creek — staying a couple of hundred feet above the trees before dropping back toward the water — aiming for the Sherpa-Argonaut basin.

Do not follow cairns out into the boulder field: published accounts specifically warn that the cairned line invites you off the better path. Stay with the creek.

Around 5,800 ft the ground steepens into sustained loose talus. The usual bivy is at the top of a talus field in the basin, and from there it is another hour and a half to two hours of talus-hopping to the toe of the ridge.

A southern approach over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek exists but is a longer, less direct way to this particular route.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
AIM FOR THE DOUBLE V AND CAMP JUST INSIDE THE LOWER ONE. Approaching the Sherpa-Argonaut col from the basin, the skyline reads as two V-shaped notches. The bivy sits at the top of a talus field just inside the LOWER V, and that pairing — two Vs, camp inside the lower — is the most reliable landmark on this approach because it is a skyline shape rather than a feature you have to be close to.

FROM THE BASIN, THE MOVE IS WEST-NORTHWEST AND UP A DEEP GULLY. Ascend talus west-northwest to a deep gully that runs to a NOTCH on the ridge at about 7,000 ft. That gully is the way onto the route; contour up and climber's RIGHT out of the basin to reach the base of that lower notch.

ARRIVAL: at the notch there are easy slabs that can be scrambled before you rope up. Easy slabs at a notch at roughly 7,000 ft, reached by a gully, with about 1,500 ft of ridge above you — that is the start.

WHAT GETTING IT WRONG LOOKS LIKE, and it is expensive here: the ridge is largely Class 2-4 and you want to stay JUST ON THE EAST SIDE OF THE CREST. Straying onto the crest itself at the wrong point adds unavoidable 5.6-5.8 pitches on a route that is already long. So a party that gains the ridge somewhere other than the notch will find the climbing immediately harder than advertised — that is the signal to downclimb and traverse rather than to press on.

CONFIRMATION LOW ON THE ROUTE: the first section ends with a roughly 25 m rappel from slings into a notch. If you have climbed a long way with no rappel, you are not on the ridge proper.
hazards: Sustained loose talus above 5,800 ft, more tedious than technical but a long way
Misleading cairns that pull you off the creek into the boulder field
Blowdown on the unmaintained climbers' path
Straying onto the crest and adding unprotectable 5.6-5.8 ground
Large detached blocks making protection difficult on the upper pitches
A descent that is not a reversal of the route and is considered its trickiest part

approach_variants.name: Longs Pass and Ingalls Creek to the Sherpa-Argonaut basin and Table Rock
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep once the gully system above Ingalls Creek is dry
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda / Longs Pass trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take Longs Pass Trail #1229 through open pine and sage switchbacks about 2.5 miles and 1,950 ft to Longs Pass at roughly 6,200-6,400 ft.

Drop off the north side on the steep eroded boot path, losing 1,400-1,600 ft over about a mile to Ingalls Creek at roughly 4,800 ft. Ford the creek — a rock-hop in low water, a real wet crossing in snowmelt — and follow the Ingalls Creek Trail west about half a mile to the Beverly-Turnpike junction at about 4,700 ft. That junction is the last dependable water before the alpine basin.

A climbers' boot path switchbacks up through forest and talus from there; around 6,000 ft it narrows into a gully system. Traverse east several hundred feet to a divide between two gullies and drop into the EASTERN one, which leads toward Sherpa. Class 2 slopes above it reach Table Rock, a large flat boulder at about 7,400 ft in the Sherpa-Argonaut basin and the usual high bivy.

Carry all your water above the Beverly-Turnpike junction; the upper basin is dry.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A FREE-STANDING PILLAR, NOT A FACE, AND THAT IS WHY THIS ONE CANNOT BE MISTAKEN ONCE YOU ARE CLOSE. From Table Rock a short Class 3 scramble gains a notch just WEST of Sherpa's summit on the range divide, putting you on the crest EAST of the balanced rock. Follow the crest west over blocks and sandy exposed benches at Class 3-4 until you are standing at the foot of a detached granite pillar. That pillar is the route.

THE MOVE AT THE BASE IS THE PROOF: you cannot simply start climbing.
