Gaining the pedestal at the bottom needs a shoulder-stand off a partner, or a rope thrown or lassoed over the point of the pedestal. If you have found a start you can climb unaided, you are on the peak's ordinary ridge scrambling and not on this feature.

SECOND CONFIRMATION, AND IT IS UNUSUAL FOR THE RANGE: above the pedestal the climbing is BOLT-PROTECTED FRICTION at about 5.7 to a flat top, with a single ageing bolt up there used to rappel back down. Bolts on Sherpa are rare enough that finding them is strong positive evidence.

DIRECTION CHECK IN CLOUD: you arrive at the crest EAST of the pillar and walk WEST to it. If you are heading east along the crest you are walking toward Sherpa's true summit and away from the rock.

AND A SCOPE WARNING WORTH READING BEFORE YOU COMMIT: this is not a route up the mountain. It is the technical feature near the summit, and most parties combine it with the Class 3-4 ridge traverse to Sherpa's main summit. If your objective was the peak, the pillar is an add-on rather than the way up.
hazards: A steep, loose descent off Longs Pass in both directions
An Ingalls Creek ford that is a genuine crossing in early-season snowmelt
Loose rockfall-prone gully and basin terrain — helmets strongly advised
A dry upper basin: no water above the Beverly-Turnpike junction
An exposed Class 3-4 crest traverse to reach the pillar
A single ageing bolt as the rappel anchor off the top
The unroped downclimb back to camp can take as long as the technical pitch itself

approach_variants.name: Beverly Turnpike and Fourth Creek Pass to an Ingalls Creek camp, then straight up the south side
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The brush is the reason: it is impassably wet in early season and the gully may hold snow in the shoulders
approach_variants.notes:
From the Beverly Turnpike trailhead at the end of FR-9737-112 off the North Fork Teanaway Road, at about 0.5 mile bear left onto signed Trail #1391. Taking the Bean Creek fork here is a commonly reported mistake, so read the sign.

At about 3.1 miles turn right onto Trail #1226.1, the Fourth Creek Trail; at about 3.6 miles you crest Fourth Creek Pass with the first open views of Argonaut, Colchuck and Dragontail. Descend the far side to roughly 6 miles and 4,200 ft, ford Ingalls Creek, and camp at the Fourth Creek confluence. Day one is about 6 miles and 2,000 ft.

From camp, follow the Ingalls Creek Trail west about half a mile, then cut sharply left and north and climb straight upslope. Expect roughly 300 vertical feet of tangled forest and then close to 1,000 ft of dense slide alder above that — progress can drop to a few hundred feet an hour.

At about 5,200 ft the brush relents. Climb the LEFT side of a large drainage gully to about 6,600 ft, then the gully itself.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TWO TESTS, ONE AT THE GULLY FORK AND ONE AT THE WALL, AND YOU NEED BOTH.

FIRST, THE FORK AT ABOUT 7,100 FT. The gully you have been climbing splits. The standard line is the LEFT branch. The right branch also reaches the mountain but is far less travelled, so a party that drifts right will find progressively less sign of passage — that absence is the signal to come back down and cross over.

SECOND, THE WALL ITSELF, and this is the one that matters in fog because the gully fork can be ambiguous under snow. At the base of the south face there are TWO SHORT LEFT-FACING CORNERS side by side. The route starts in the RIGHTMOST AND LARGER of the two. Not a corner — two corners, and you take the bigger, right-hand one. If there is only one corner in front of you, you are not at the start.

WHAT THE CLIMBING SHOULD FEEL LIKE, as a check on all of the above: blocky, generally solid rock, three pitches, graded 5.6 — but an old-school 5.6 that parties consistently report climbing like modern 5.9 or harder. So sustained-feeling climbing is NOT evidence you are off route here. Watch for a few loose blocks low down.

A SEPARATE FEATURE WORTH NOT CONFUSING WITH THE START: high on the mountain there is a 50-foot gully with a chockstone near its top, Class 4, taken by stepping right at the overhang, which tops out on the east ridge a short way from the summit. That is the finish of the ordinary scramble line, and this catalog's stored approach text for this route describes it as though it were the route. It is not the base of the 5.6 face climb, and a party navigating to it will end up on the scramble.
hazards: Close to 1,000 ft of dense slide alder above 300 ft of jackstraw forest — the defining feature of the day
An Ingalls Creek ford that can be cold and swift early, and ice-covered in the shoulders
Loose blocks low on the route
Possible snow in the gully in the shoulder seasons — carry axe and crampons if in doubt
The descent rappels a chockstone gully where ropes are reported to hang up on the chockstone
A heavily worn sling anchor above that chockstone: inspect and back it up

approach_variants.name: Mountaineer Creek off-trail to the basin under Argonaut's north face
approach_variants.season: Roughly Apr-Jun as a snow climb; consistent snow starts around 4,700 ft in a normal spring
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead, follow the trail past the Colchuck Lake split and then leave it, heading up toward Argonaut's north side. There is no maintained path for this and route choice through the lower ground is yours: the terrain is swampy in places, there is a log crossing of the creek, and there is a notorious slide-alder slope that is best avoided by taking nearby talus instead.

Consistent snow generally starts around 4,700 ft. Above that, follow the drainage up toward the north face; parties have used snowshoes for much of this section.

Nothing published gives a reliable trailhead-to-base time for this approach, and the accounts that do quote figures are quoting whole days that also include a traverse of Colchuck, so no figure is given here.

The couloir above runs a constant, sustained 35-50 degrees for about 1,200 ft with no significant steps, narrowing as it goes, and exits on mid-fifth-class or icy ground onto the summit ridge system.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COULOIR THAT NARROWS IS THE RIGHT ONE. This is the most useful in-fog property of the line: it holds a constant angle for its whole length and it TAPERS, from roughly fifty feet wide at the bottom to as little as ten feet near the top. A gully that stays the same width, or that has obvious steps and pitches in it, is not this feature.

ORIENTATION AGAINST THE ROCK: the couloir sits immediately EAST of the Northeast Buttress, so from inside the couloir the buttress rock is the bounding rib on its WEST side. Standing at the entrance with a defined rock rib to the west and open snow slopes to the east is the correct position; standing with rock on both sides in a short, steep slot means you are in one of the minor gullies rather than the main line.

AND THE EXIT AS A CONFIRMATION: this couloir does NOT run to the summit. It finishes with one mid-fifth-class or icy pitch onto the summit-ridge system, followed by third and fourth class scrambling to distinctive A-frame summit blocks. A line that appears to run straight to the top is a different feature.

HONEST LIMIT, STATED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER: published accounts of this approach describe reaching the base without naming a landmark that distinguishes it from neighbouring gullies at close range — one first-hand report simply says they reached the base of the couloir. The shape of the couloir and the buttress on its west are real, corroborated tests; a specific arrival marker at the toe is not published and none is invented here. Scout the face from lower in the basin in good visibility before committing in the dark.
hazards: A notorious slide-alder slope on the approach, best bypassed on talus
A log crossing of Mountaineer Creek and swampy ground below the snowline
1,200 ft of sustained 35-50 degree snow with avalanche and rockfall exposure as the day warms
A mid-fifth-class or icy exit pitch
A descent involving rappels down slabs and a traverse of a wet ledge into the east gully
No maintained trail on the approach and no reliable published timing for it

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake, the Aasgard trail, then left through the brush to the base gully
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the traverse above the lake holds wet snow into July and has produced serious slips
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead on FR 7601, take the Colchuck Lake Trail #1599 — four miles and 2,280 ft, a log-bridge crossing of Mountaineer Creek at about 1.5 miles, right at the Lake Stuart junction, then a boulder-moraine finish to the outlet in about two and a half to three hours. Fill water here; it is the last source.

Head round toward the lake's south and east side onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail and gain talus and heather to about 400 ft above the lake, thirty to forty minutes.

Then leave it: break climber's LEFT through a dense band of slide alder and heather, fifteen to twenty minutes of real bushwhacking, to the obvious gully leading up to Colchuck Balanced Rock. The final scramble to the wall is loose third and fourth class; rope up if in doubt.

Reckon three and a half to four hours car to base.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE MARKER IS A BOLT WITH A BLACK HANGER ABOUT EIGHT FEET UP A LEFT-FACING CORNER, AND IT IS THE ONLY UNAMBIGUOUS THING AT THE BASE OF THIS WALL. Get to it in three steps.

STEP ONE — THE SANDY LEDGE. Scramble the base gully as for the wall's ordinary line until you reach the sandy ledge that every route here starts from. If you have not found a sandy ledge, you are still in the approach gully.

STEP TWO — TEN FEET AND STEP LEFT. From the sandy ledge, climb about ten feet of easy ground and step LEFT onto a small ledge. There is a TREE on it. A small ledge with a tree, one short step left of the sandy ledge, is the belay.

STEP THREE — LOOK UP. Above that ledge is a LEFT-FACING CORNER with a bolt roughly eight feet off the deck carrying a BLACK HANGER. That bolt is the confirmation, and it is why this route is worth a base finding while its neighbours are not: it is a fixed, findable object rather than a relative position.

WHERE THIS SITS ON THE WALL: to the LEFT of both the ordinary west face line and the harder line beside it. So if you never stepped left off the sandy ledge, you are on one of those two instead.

GRADE CHECK ON THE FIRST MOVES: getting off the ground is thoughtful 5.11 with a second punchy section midway. The wall's ordinary line starts far easier. If the first moves are casual, you are not on this route.

AND A RETREAT FACT WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU LEAVE THE GROUND: the anchor at the top of the fourth pitch is the last point from which a rope reaches back down — two 40 m rappels return you to the base gully from there, with an intermediate anchor if your rope is short. Above it you are committed to finishing over the top.
hazards: A wet-snow traverse above Colchuck Lake into July with a history of serious slips
Fifteen to twenty minutes of dense slide alder and heather to reach the gully
Loose third and fourth class scrambling in the base gully with parties above
No water above Colchuck Lake
Above the fourth-pitch anchor there is no rappel retreat — the route must be finished
A long walk-off round the peak after topping out

approach_variants.name: Snow Lakes trail to Perfection Lake, Prusik Pass and the Druid Plateau
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the cross-country section above Prusik Pass frequently holds snow into July
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Snow Lakes trailhead, about four miles up Icicle Creek Road from Leavenworth. Follow Snow Lakes Trail #1553 through burn-scarred forest and switchbacks above Icicle Creek, past Nada and Snow Lakes at roughly six to seven miles, and on into the core basin — Lake Viviane, Leprechaun, Sprite, then Perfection Lake, by which point you have covered eight or nine miles and about 4,500 ft.

At the north side of Perfection Lake, leave the main trail on the scramblers' path that switchbacks up to Prusik Pass at about 7,460-7,500 ft. That junction is easy to miss and the pass is the last reliable water.

From the pass everything is cross-country. Contour northwest across talus and heather benches at roughly 7,300-7,400 ft, keeping to the WEST side of the Lorelei Lakelets, then north to a broad rib at about 7,900-8,000 ft. From just below 8,000 ft turn northwest and climb steep talus and scree onto the Druid Plateau at about 8,350 ft.

There are no cairns and no tread above Prusik Pass. Round trip is 30-plus miles with 7,300-plus ft of gain, so essentially everyone camps.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SUMMIT BLOCK IS A SEPARATE OBJECT AND THE PLATEAU IS NOT THE TOP. This is the failure mode on Cannon: parties gain the Druid Plateau at about 8,350 ft, find themselves on broad high ground, and treat arriving there as arriving. The actual climbing is a distinct BLOCK that only comes into view once you are on the plateau, across it to the west.

SO THE TEST IS: can you see a discrete block of rock standing above the plateau surface? If you are on flat or gently rolling ground with nothing obviously above you, you have not crossed the plateau yet. Cross it and take the WESTERN slopes to the foot of the block.

WHICH SIDE OF THE BLOCK, AND THIS IS THE PART THAT MATTERS IN CLOUD: the way up is a RAMP on the block's SOUTH side. It is the last fifteen feet or so to the true summit, low-angle friction slab with almost no positive holds. If you have walked round the block and found only steep unfriendly rock, you are on the wrong aspect — keep going round to the south.

WHAT THE RIGHT GROUND FEELS LIKE: this is a friction problem, not a hold problem. Approach shoes with good rubber, or rock shoes, make a real difference, and the downclimb of the same ramp is the psychological crux of the day for most parties because low-angle slab is harder to read going down.

STAGING CHECK BELOW THE PLATEAU: from Prusik Pass you should pass the Lorelei Lakelets on their WEST side and reach a broad rib around 7,900-8,000 ft before turning northwest. If you passed the lakelets on their east, you are drifting toward the wrong drainage.
hazards: No cairns and no tread above Prusik Pass — serious route-finding on talus and heather
Snow frequently lingering on the cross-country section into July
An exposed, holdless friction slab for the final fifteen feet, harder to downclimb than to climb
Verglas on shaded ground into July, adding real exposure to otherwise easy terrain
No bail-out shelter: sun, lightning and afternoon storms on open high ground
Core Zone overnight permits are competitive and effectively required

approach_variants.name: Stuart Lake trailhead and the Cannon Creek basin — the shorter, rougher side
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the lower cross-country section is brushy and holds snow later than the trail does
approach_variants.notes:
The documented alternative reaches the same staging ground near the Druid Plateau from the north instead, out of the Stuart Lake trailhead: up the Mountaineer Creek valley and then cross-country into the Cannon Creek basin.

This is much shorter than the Snow Lakes walk, and that is the whole of its appeal. It is also markedly rougher: the lower section is brushy and there are cliff bands to negotiate, and there is no trail for any of it.

Cannon has no maintained trail to its summit by any line, so both approaches end in the same cross-country problem. What differs is how much of the day is spent on tread before that starts — nearly all of it on the Snow Lakes side, very little on this one.

No reliable published time or distance exists for this variant and none is given. Treat it as a full day of navigation rather than a walk with a scramble at the end.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
BOTH APPROACHES CONVERGE ON THE DRUID PLATEAU, SO THE BASE TEST IS IDENTICAL AND THE ARRIVAL TEST IS NOT. Coming from the north you reach the plateau area from the Cannon Creek basin rather than from Prusik Pass, so the Lorelei Lakelets and the broad rib are NOT on your route and cannot be used to confirm position — do not try to apply the southern approach's landmarks here.

WHAT STILL HOLDS: the summit block is a distinct object standing above the plateau, reached across the plateau on its WESTERN slopes, and the way up it is a low-angle friction ramp on its SOUTH side, roughly the last fifteen feet to the true summit. Almost no positive holds. That is the base, and it is the same base for anyone who gets here.

THE NORTH-SIDE-SPECIFIC WARNING: the ground below the basin has CLIFF BANDS in it. Unlike the southern route, where the navigation problem is featureless open talus, here it is possible to be cliffed out and to have to lose height to get round. If you are on steepening ground with the basin still above you, come down and traverse rather than pushing on.

AND A ROUTE-CHOICE NOTE: the northeast ridge is a separate line on this mountain and is described as an ascent route only, with most parties descending the Prusik Pass side. If you have come up from the north expecting to reverse it, check which line you are actually on before committing to that plan.
hazards: Brushy lower cross-country with cliff bands to negotiate and no trail
No cairns or tread anywhere on the upper mountain
An exposed holdless friction ramp on the summit block
Snow and verglas on shaded ground into July
No published timing for this variant — plan conservatively
No bail-out shelter on the high ground

approach_variants.name: Eightmile trailhead and the burned slopes to the northeast ridge crest
approach_variants.season: Mid to late summer, once the snow is off the ridge and out of the ground around Coney Lake
approach_variants.notes:
From US-2 at the west end of Leavenworth, follow Icicle Road about eight miles, then turn left onto the signed gravel Eightmile Road, cross Icicle Creek and climb about 1,100 ft to the large lot at the road end. A Northwest Forest Pass is required. This route starts at the Eightmile trailhead itself, not at the Stuart Lake trailhead further up the same road system.

The route climbs steep, bushy, loose burned slopes to gain the ridge crest, then follows and traverses beneath the crest, and finishes with a talus gully and a short scramble to the summit block.

It is described in the sources as an ascent route only. Most parties come down the other side of the mountain instead — Prusik Pass, the Upper Enchantment basin, down Aasgard Pass and out via Colchuck Lake to the Stuart Lake trailhead — which makes this a demanding roughly fifteen-mile loop with sustained Class 3 and bushwhacking, at least twelve hours car to car, and two different trailheads.

Plan the car shuttle before you start walking.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TOWERS ARE THE MARKER, AND THE INSTRUCTION IS TO GO UNDER THEM. The identifying feature of this ridge is a band of towers on the crest that CANNOT be climbed directly, and the route's answer to them is a loose traverse of about a third of a mile BELOW the crest. That traverse is the route's signature and its worst ground.

SO THE TEST WHEN YOU GAIN THE CREST IS: keep going until the crest stops being walkable. When rock towers block the ridge in front of you, do not look for a way over them — drop onto the flank and traverse beneath. A party that finds itself scrambling technical rock on the crest has missed the traverse.

AND THE ARRIVAL TEST AT THE OTHER END: the traverse ends at a TALUS GULLY. Talus, after loose sidehill traversing, is the cue that the towers are behind you. From the top of that gully it is a short scramble to the summit block.

WHAT GOING TOO LOW LOOKS LIKE: the traverse is beneath the crest, not down in the basin. If you have lost enough height that the towers are well above you and you are on continuous scree, you will have to regain it — this is the most common way the traverse costs more than the third of a mile it looks like on a map.

BEFORE ANY OF THAT — THE LOWER HALF IS THE REAL PROBLEM. Steep, bushy, loose burned slopes with no path, and this route is best done in mid to late summer once the snow is gone from around Coney Lake and off the ridge. Snow on the lower slopes turns an unpleasant ascent into a serious one.

AND THE DIRECTIONAL WARNING: this is an ascent-only line. Do not plan to reverse it. The descent is over the top and down the far side of the mountain to a different trailhead.
hazards: Steep, bushy, loose burned slopes with no trail on the lower half
A third of a mile of loose traversing below a band of unclimbable towers — the crux of the route
Sustained Class 3 scrambling and bushwhacking over a roughly fifteen-mile day
Descent is over the summit to a DIFFERENT trailhead: a car shuttle or a long road walk
At least twelve hours car to car, so an early start is not optional
Snow lingering around Coney Lake and on the ridge in early summer

_SKIPPED._note: Fifteen routes with an empty approach_variants were deliberately left empty. An empty result is a real result; each reason is a statement about what is published, not about effort.
_SKIPPED.wa_mount_stuart_north_face: PHANTOM ROUTE — do not enrich. The row's own beta records that a search of Mountain Project's Mt Stuart area, SummitPost and Beckey summaries found no separately named 'North Face' route at this grade. The north side is divided among the North Ridge, Ice Cliff Glacier, Stuart Glacier Couloir and Girth Pillar, all of which have their own rows. Writing an approach for it would manufacture a base for a climb that does not exist. Same shape as the Cat Scratch Gullies row this project exists because of.
_SKIPPED.wa_der_dihedral: One shared approach with Backbone Ridge and Serpentine Arete, and the row itself says the exact line is sparsely documented, the start is not well cairned, and parties should budget extra route-finding time. The only published position is relative — 'a couple of ridgelines short of Backbone Ridge, lower on the face' — which is not an in-fog test, and inventing a marker on a rarely climbed line is exactly the failure this field exists to prevent.
_SKIPPED.wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_north_ridge: DUPLICATE ROW. Same FA party (Rick La Belle and Pat Derr, 1971), same 13 pitches, same route as wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge, filed under a different area. Enriching both would put two approaches on one climb and two different base findings on one notch. See _DEFECTS.
_SKIPPED.wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir: Filed under the Balanced Rock sub-area but describes a couloir on Sherpa Peak's northeast side. The only published identification is 'an obvious couloir on the northeast side', and the row itself notes a related pair of loosely named couloirs on the same face — so the one property that would make a base finding useful, which of several adjacent couloirs is the right one, is precisely what is not published.
_SKIPPED.wa_accendo_lunae_lib_west_face_var: Colchuck Balanced Rock. Starts at the same point in the base gully as an existing route and diverges high on the wall. There is no distinct base to find, and its published position is stated relative to a neighbouring line rather than to anything on the ground.
_SKIPPED.wa_full_tilt_tempest_wall_free_version: Colchuck Balanced Rock. Positioned only as 'a few hundred feet down the gully to the right of the West Face start', which is a relative bearing on a loose gully rather than a marker. No published feature at the start.
_SKIPPED.wa_leche_la_vaca: Colchuck Balanced Rock. The row places it 'in this same base gully area on the left side of the wall, near Scarface' — near, not at. No sourced marker at the start.
_SKIPPED.wa_milk_n_honey: Colchuck Balanced Rock. The row's own wording is 'sits in the same general wall area as The Scoop and Rikki Tikki Tavi, toward the right side of the formation'. General wall area is not a base finding.
_SKIPPED.wa_rikki_tikki_tavi: Colchuck Balanced Rock. Positioned only as 'to the right of The Scoop'. Relative to a route you also have to identify first.
_SKIPPED.wa_scarface_3: Colchuck Balanced Rock. Two published positions that do not agree — the row says 'the gully just left of the West Face route start', Mountain Project says 'several hundred feet to the right of the old NW Buttress line'. Left of one thing and right of another is not resolvable without a topo, and picking one would be inventing.
_SKIPPED.wa_the_balanced_rock: Not a ground-up climb at all: a V2 boulder problem on top of the balanced summit block, reached only after climbing one of the peak's technical routes. Its 'approach' is another route's descent. Nothing to find.
_SKIPPED.wa_prusik_peak_sail_away: Prusik. The row has an EMPTY approach field and the route was first climbed in August 2025 — too new for independent published base beta. Its pitch names are known; where P1 starts on the face relative to its neighbours is not.
_SKIPPED.wa_prusik_peak_taylor_wood_route: Prusik. Empty approach field, first climbed August 2023, same problem: the pitch sequence is documented, the position of the start on the base of the face is not.
_SKIPPED.wa_prusik_peak_prayer_for_a_friend: Prusik. Empty approach field. The published detail is entirely about the pitches and the 5.14a headwall; nothing locates the start along the base.
_SKIPPED.wa_prusik_peak_alpine_craggers_delight: Prusik. Empty approach field. Described only as an 80-ft single pitch that finishes where another route's P1 ends — i.e. located relative to a route above it, not to anything on the ground.

_DEFECTS._note: Data defects noticed in passing while reading these rows. Reported, not fixed — this batch writes only approach_variants.
_DEFECTS.duplicate_sherpa_north_ridge: wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_north_ridge and wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge share an FA party (Rick La Belle and Pat Derr, 1971), a pitch count (13) and a route description. Two rows, one climb, filed under two different areas.
_DEFECTS.duplicate_prusik_south_face: wa_stanley_burgner (5.10a, 6p) and wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanley (III 5.9+, 6p) look like the same climb under its two conventional name orders. The second already has approach_variants; the first did not, which is how the pair surfaced. Confirm before either is deleted — the grades differ.
_DEFECTS.possible_duplicate_stuart_north_ridge: wa_the_direct_north_ridge_w_gendarme (5.9+, 20p) and wa_mount_stuart_north_ridge 'North Ridge (Complete)' (IV 5.9, 20p) may be one climb. wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme (5.9, 18p) is NOT a duplicate of either — it genuinely starts at the notch above the Stuart Glacier and skips about 1,200 ft, which is the whole distinction this batch's base findings turn on.
_DEFECTS.phantom_row_stuart_north_face: wa_mount_stuart_north_face is almost certainly not a real named route; the row's own beta says so. Candidate for deletion after confirming nothing else references it.
_DEFECTS.colchuck_east_ridge_direction_error: wa_colchuck_peak_east_ridge's approach says 'From Colchuck Lake, traverse northeast to the east ridge base'. Colchuck Peak lies SOUTH-WEST of the lake and the col at the foot of the east ridge lies south-east of the summit. Traversing northeast from the lake walks away from the mountain.
_DEFECTS.argonaut_south_face_two_routes_in_one_ro: wa_south_face_12's approach text describes the ordinary south-side scramble finishing up a 50-ft chockstone gully to the east ridge, while its beta describes a 3-pitch 5.6 rock climb starting at two left-facing corners. Those read as two different lines sharing a row.
_DEFECTS.gorillas_wall_aspect_mislabelled_in_pros: The approach text shared by wa_gorillas_direct and wa_the_direct_north_ridge_w_gendarme calls the Gorillas wall 'the South Face'. Sources consistently call it the West Face Wall and the rows' own aspect column says W. The prose sends parties to the wrong aspect of the mountain.
_DEFECTS.sherpa_balanced_rock_trailhead_disagreem: wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_standard's approach text describes the Longs Pass / Esmeralda trailhead on the Teanaway side, while its waypoints list the Stuart Lake trailhead on the Icicle side as waypoint zero — opposite sides of the range. This is the audit:trailhead-agreement shape, in the waypoints rather than in approach_logistics.
_DEFECTS.beckey_davis_trailhead_note_contradicts_: wa_beckey_davis's Stuart Lake Trailhead waypoint carries a note saying it is 'alternate access only, used when the standard Stuart Lake Trailhead approach is closed', and then names the Stuart Lake Trailhead as the standard. The note appears to have been written for the Snow Lakes trailhead and attached to the wrong waypoint.
_DEFECTS.upper_north_ridge_trailhead_flagged_in_i: wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme's waypoint note already records that the DB lists the Stuart Lake trailhead while this variant is documented from the Ingalls Lake side. The approach_logistics still says Esmeralda; the two halves of the row have been reconciled in opposite directions at different times.
